newsitem.title: GERMANY: Oder officials say Bonn flood aid insufficient.
newsitem.headline: Oder officials say Bonn flood aid insufficient.

text.p: Officials in Germany's Oder River region said on Wednesday 500 million marks ($270 million) in flood aid pledged by Bonn probably fell short of the mark and billions would be needed.

Local officials said the money might be enough initially, but that in the long run compensation claims for homes and businesses as well as a reconstruction programme to reinforce flood barriers along the Oder would entail much more.
"The money will not be enough. I am quite sure of this," Brandenburg state's environment minister Matthias Platzeck told Berlin's InfoRadio.

"We can only assess the full extent of the damage and work needed once the water has gone...We should wait a while longer so that we can work with concrete figures. But certainly it will be billions of marks worth of damage," Platzeck said.

In addition to the government aid -- announced by Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Tuesday in a special statement on the crisis -- millions of marks in donations have poured in for flood victims in more than a dozen bank accounts.
A government reconstruction agency has made 200 million marks available for low-interest credits in the region.
The federal government and regional authorities have set aside a combined 40 million marks for immediate flood relief.
Families who were forced to leave their water-logged homes are entitled to 2,000 marks while businesses may receive 10,000 marks to cover immediate costs and losses.
Brandenburg's finance minister Wilma Simon highlighted another potential problem, saying that authorities would have to do their best to distribute funds with an even hand.
She said many donations, though generous, were directed to specific interest groups and sometimes failed to address the plight of those most in need.

Wilma said one example was that pop star Michael Jackson had donated money to a nursery school in Ratzdorf, one the first of Germany's Oder villages to be hit by floods, but in fact there was no kindergarten there.
"We will not be able to prevent certain people, who have featured in the media, from getting more aid than what they have actually lost," Simon said.

Local officials in the region on Germany's eastern border said it would be a long time before they could assess the precise amount of damage to individuals and businesses and the compensation and reconstruction costs.
Kohl, who described the flooding in the past weeks as the "worst natural disaster ever faced by newly-unified Germany", did not specify how the 500 million marks would be broken down.
The Oder was swollen by the same rains that caused flooding in the Czech Republic and Poland last month, claiming more than 100 lives and causing billions of dollars' worth of damage.
Germany has escaped the worst of the floods, but damage to homes, businesses and farms has been extensive.
The swollen River Oder retreated steadily throughout Wednesday, leaving behind a vast trail of mud, dead fish and waterlogged homes.

Three weeks of flooding, the region's worst in living memory, have turned a large tract of once-fertile agricultural land in the Ziltendorf basin south of Frankfurt an der Oder into a vast mosquito-infested swamp.

The stench of stagnant water hangs over the area. An eery silence pervades the villages of Aurith, Wiesenau and Brieskow-Finkenheerd still largely submerged to the rooftops after a dike broke last month and residents were evacuated.

Many evacuees are desperate to return to salvage what they can of their homes. But even now the water is retreating, German officials have warned residents not to return too soon to these ghost towns on the Oder.
